idiom_name: class whose data lives in class-level storage with non-static accessor methods
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep every data member at class level (static members, class variables, companion-object fields, or module-scope state) and keep the accessor methods non-static, so any constructed instance reads and writes the same storage while its own identity stays independent. Where the language has no class-level storage, move the state to the module or translation-unit scope and let ordinary functions or methods operate on it. Keep the storage private, treat every write as a concurrent write, and document on the type that all instances share state - nothing in the signature says so. Provide a reset seam for tests (or the state cannot be isolated), and hide the storage behind a small holder so it can later be replaced by an injected instance without changing call sites.
code_sketch:
client code:   a = new Settings();  b = new Settings()
               a.setLevel(3);   b.getLevel()      # 3 - same storage
implementation:
    class Settings
        private static level                # one slot per program
        void setLevel(v):  level = v        # non-static method ...
        int  getLevel():   return level     # ... over static data
    # keep the storage private, synchronize writes, document the sharing
pitfalls: Making the fields static while the class behaves as if instances were independent: the class must document that all instances share state, because nothing in the signature says so.
Forgetting synchronization: shared state is concurrent state in any language with threads, and every write needs a guard.
No reset seam: tests inherit each other's mutations unless a documented reset path exists.

Wrong move: put request, tenant or async-task context in a monostate -> concurrent work overwrites shared state and tests leak across cases -> instead use request-scoped injection or context-local storage.

Wrong move: confuse C++ std::monostate with the Monostate pattern -> std::monostate is an empty std::variant alternative, not shared mutable storage -> instead use an explicit state holder for shared configuration (or std::optional for absence).

Wrong move: reuse one EnTT monostate key with incompatible value types -> reads and writes no longer describe one stable slot and can be undefined -> instead allocate distinct keys/types and wrap configuration behind a typed API.
